name: Penumbra Crag
specific_features: Ancient survey markers of pre-human origin
description: Penumbra Crag is a world of sharp edges and deep shadows, its surface carved into networks of razor-edged ridges that divide the terrain into a mosaic of narrow valleys permanently shaded by the surrounding rock walls. The ridges are composed of hardened igneous stone that has resisted the thin atmosphere's erosion while softer surrounding rock has been scoured away. Wind-carved hoodoo formations stand like sentinels along the valley floors, their shapes grotesque and suggestive.

The thin atmosphere carries a constant dust-laden wind that hisses across the ridge tops and howls through the narrow valleys. In the shadow valleys, temperatures plunge far below freezing even during daylight hours, as the ridges block all direct starlight. The result is a world of extreme local temperature variation, where a few steps from shadow to sunlight can mean a temperature difference of eighty degrees.

Pre-human survey markers have been discovered at regular intervals along the major ridge lines, carved into the rock with tools that left perfectly circular bore-holes. The markers contain no inscriptions or symbols, only geometric patterns of holes arranged in grids. Their purpose remains unknown: they may be navigational aids, territorial markers, or something entirely outside human conceptual frameworks. Carbon dating of mineral deposits within the bore-holes places their creation at approximately 1.2 million years ago.

Penumbra Crag's metallic resources are substantial but distributed throughout the ridge network, requiring extensive surface operations to extract. The ancient survey markers have prompted calls for protected status that conflict with mining proposals. A compromise has been proposed designating the marked ridges as archaeological preserves while opening unmarked regions to extraction, but enforcement in the labyrinthine terrain would be nearly impossible.
